reviews.evidence: The core is a two-point law specified by its PMF; PMF is the only direct reusable definition. Expectation and variance are later properties, so they remain ordinary links.

The theorem hypotheses explicitly use iid variables, expectation, finite variance, and a normal limiting law; all four are direct prerequisites. Distributional convergence is notation in the statement and has no canonical knowl here.
The defining expression is an expectation of exp(itX), so expectation is a direct ingredient in addition to the random variable. Distribution and MGF are later consequences/comparisons.

The statement assumes a random variable with finite expectation and variance and bounds its deviation probability; these three prerequisites match the core. Markov and weak-law links are proof/application material.
The bound is stated using E[e^{tX}] and a random variable, so expectation is direct. Markov and MGF are identified as derivation/context later and are not required to parse the statement.

The definition requires an integrable random variable, a probability space, measurable Y, indicator products, and uniqueness up to a.e. equality. Integrability and a.e. equality were missing from the direct prerequisite boundary.
The core normalizes covariance by the two variances and assumes both are finite and nonzero; variance is therefore a direct prerequisite alongside covariance and random variables.

The core is an expectation of a centered product for two random variables with finite second moments. Random-variable and expectation prerequisites supply the definition; variance and independence occur only as later identities/properties.

The core defines K_X as log of the MGF for a random variable on an interval around zero. Function, random variable, and MGF are exactly the direct ingredients; cumulants and independence are later properties.
The definition is the nth derivative at zero of an existing cumulant generating function. Random variable and CGF suffice; expectation, variance, and additivity are later consequences.
The core defines F(t)=P((-infinity,t]) for a probability measure on R. The later random-variable, PMF, and PDF representations do not belong in the minimal definition's prerequisite list.

The core is explicitly for an R^d-valued random variable and integrates f log f against Lebesgue measure. Random-vector, Lebesgue integration, Lebesgue measure, and PDF are direct; scalar random-variable was too weak.
The core assigns P(A) to an event in a probability space. Probability space and probability measure provide the ambient triple and assignment; measurable-set is explanatory later.

The identity equates expectation over the original space with integration against the law, for measurable g and integrable g(X). Expectation is a direct operation in the theorem and was missing; the law and measurability mappings remain direct.

The core is the Lebesgue integral of an integrable random variable. Random-variable, Lebesgue integral, and integrable-function prerequisites match the definition; variance and covariance are later uses.

The theorem compares KL divergence of two probability measures on a sigma-algebra and proves nonnegativity. Probability measure, set, sigma-algebra, and KL definition are direct; Pinsker is a later application.
The definition compares the laws of two random variables. Random-variable and distribution-law are necessary and sufficient; independence and moments are explicitly later distinctions.

The core requires a sequence on one probability space, independent variables, identical laws, and the distribution-law equivalence. Every listed prerequisite is used in that definition; limit theorems are later applications.

The core defines event independence by factorization on a probability space. Conditional probability, sigma-algebra independence, and variable independence are later equivalent extensions, so the probability-space-only boundary is appropriate.
The definition quantifies over Borel sets for random variables on a probability space, requiring the Borel sigma-algebra. Generated sigma-algebra and event formulations are later equivalences.
